newsitem.title: USA: GM, NBC, U.S. Olympic Committee in deal.
newsitem.headline: GM, NBC, U.S. Olympic Committee in deal.

text.p: General Motors Corp, NBC Inc and the U.S. Olympic Committee said Wednesday the automaker had agreed to a landmark media and sponsorship agreement.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed, but the three parties said in a statement that the pact represents a "multimillion-dollar investment" by GM.
The agreement, which designates GM as the official domestic car and truck of the U.S. Olympic team, runs through the 2008 Olympic Games.
NBC, a unit of General Electric Co, has the broadcast rights to the Games from 2000 through to 2008.
The GM deal does not designate GM as the sole automotive sponsor for the USOC, said John Krimsky, USOC deputy secretary general. He said the USOC would have one other car sponsor.

During a news conference with Krimsky, Philip Guarascio, GM vice president and general manager of North American operations, marketing and advertising, and Dick Ebersol, president of NBC Sports, all declined to say what the value of the sponsorship and the TV advertising would be.
However, speaking to reporters after the news conference, Krimsky said that reports putting the value between $500 million and $1 billion were "very much in the ballpark."

A GM official who declined to be identified said the total could come close to $1 billion. He said it would depend on such factors as how much advertising GM finally bought and the value of the cars that were used during the Olympics.
Ebersol said NBC would announce three or four more significant agreements in the fourth quarter.
Krimsky said negotiations with AT&T Corp were pretty far along. AT&T said Tuesday it was in discussions on a multi-year deal.

Ebersol said planning for the 2000 Summer Games in Sydney, Australia, were in full swing and that NBC planned to offer 320 hours of Olympic programming on NBC Television as well as its cable networks.
Guarascio said GM had decided on a multi-year deal because it offered the most "cost effective" way to market its various car brands.
With GM currently planning for new models for future years, Guarascio said the future Olympics would provide a good forum for advertising the vehicles.
"It's a perfect fit for us, and you can take that to the bank," Guarascio said.
While NBC will only begin airing the Olympics with the 2000 Games, Krimsky said the agreement with GM is effective immediately.
The news conference was held in NBC's "Today Show" studio at New York's Rockefeller Center, with the network trying to create some pre-Olympic excitement.

Two Olympians, Dan O'Brien, who competed in the Decathlon in Atlanta last year, and Dominique Dawes, who won a gold in gymnastics last year, trotted onto the stage to deliver Olympic torches to Guarascio and Ebersol.
About a dozen other Olympians stood outside the studios in Rockefeller Center during the news conference.
